draft.title: Writing an aim and hypothesis
card: A statement of what the investigation will find out. It is often written as "To investigate how X affects Y".
A prediction that can be tested. A good one links the independent variable (the one you change) to the dependent variable (the one you measure).
A good hypothesis can be shown wrong by the results. A statement that no result could contradict cannot be tested.
A hypothesis is often written as "If the independent variable is changed, then the dependent variable will change in this way".
draft.remember: The aim says what you will find out. The hypothesis predicts the link between the two variables and can be tested.

a.q: Which of these is a hypothesis that could be tested in an investigation?
opts: If the water is hotter, then sugar will dissolve faster
To find out how temperature affects how fast sugar dissolves
Sugar and water are used in many kitchens and laboratories
Sugar might dissolve faster, or it might not dissolve faster
a.why: The first option predicts how changing temperature will change dissolving time, so results could show it wrong. The second is an aim: it says what will be found out but makes no prediction. The last cannot be shown wrong, because any result fits it.
a.clue: Look for a prediction linking a changed variable to a measured one.

b.q: Ravi wants to know how the height of a ramp affects how far a toy car rolls. Which hypothesis is best?
opts: If the ramp is higher, then the car will roll further
If the ramp is changed, then the car will do something
The car will roll further on a smooth floor than a rough one
To investigate how ramp height affects the distance rolled
b.why: The first option names ramp height as the variable changed and distance as the variable measured, and gives a direction that results could contradict. The second is too vague to be shown wrong. The last is an aim, not a prediction.
b.clue: Which option names both variables and could be shown wrong?

a.best: If the water is hotter, then sugar will dissolve faster

b.best: If the ramp is higher, then the car will roll further

problems.detail: The why refers to options by position ('first', 'second', 'last'), but the options are shuffled. In the order shown, the 'first' option is the aim and the 'last' is the kitchens statement, so the why contradicts what students see. It also never explains the 'Sugar and water are used in many kitchens' option.

The why refers to options by position ('first', 'second', 'last'), which does not match the shuffled order shown. It also never explains the smooth-floor option. That option is a testable hypothesis, but it is about floor surface rather than Ravi's variable, ramp height. Students need to be told why it is not best.

A hypothesis is often written as "If the independent variable is changed, then the dependent variable will change in this way". It should use the same variables as the aim.
